draft.briefing: Hey, you're in Beypore! Carpenters here have built wooden ships called uru by hand for centuries, without any drawings. Some are still sold to buyers in the Gulf.
draft.hungryLine: Beypore eats fish straight off the boats. Ask what came in today.

moodReplies.show-me-around: Visit an uru-building yard, then walk out on the long breakwater into the sea.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Walk to the end of the Pulimuttu breakwater and watch the river meet the sea.
moodReplies.surprise-me: Vaikom Muhammad Basheer, one of Malayalam's best-loved writers, lived here. People still call him the Sultan of Beypore.

legends.title: Ships built by memory
legends.body: Uru builders learn by working alongside their elders. The measurements are passed down by eye and memory, not plans.

legends.title: The Sultan of Beypore
legends.body: Basheer wrote many of his famous stories here, under a mangosteen tree in his yard.

tips.title: Walk the breakwater in the evening.
tips.body: The sun sets right at the end of it.

tips.title: Uru replicas make good souvenirs.
tips.body: Small models are sold in town.

story.title: Shipbuilders of the coast
story.body: Beypore's carpenters were building trading ships for Arab merchants long before Europeans came.

story.title: Tipu's port
story.body: Tipu Sultan planned a port here and called it Sultan Pattanam.

story.title: The railway that wasn't
story.body: Beypore was meant to be the end of the Madras railway line, but the plan moved to Kozhikode.

story.title: Basheer's Beypore
story.body: The writer Vaikom Muhammad Basheer made his home here, and Beypore became a pilgrimage for readers.

story.title: Your turn
story.body: Watch an uru take shape, walk the breakwater, and eat what the boats brought in. Tell me how big the ship you saw was.
